statements.quote: The history of AI is not a straight line leading inevitably to the Large Language Model.
It is a convergence of ideas from unrelated fields that were never intended to meet.
Statistical methods developed by astronomers to map the stars now weigh the next word in a sequence.
For example, GPU architectures designed for video games provide the parallel computation required for neural networks, which was never intended for AI use but worked out in the end in favour of it.
This document traces the lineage that produced modern LLMs, and tries to check out all paths that lead to it (and where else they lead to).
If you want to *see* this convergence, [The Atlas](atlas.php) places every person, place, institution and event of this history as a dot on an interactive globe — with the threads between them.

Long before digital computers existed, physicists \citeauthor{lenz1920} and his student \citeauthor{ising1925} introduced what is now recognized as the first recurrent neural network architecture .

The Ising model describes a lattice of nodes (spins) with feedback connections, where each node influences its neighbors, and the system settles into an equilibrium state in response to input conditions.
While it was designed to model ferromagnetism, not computation, its mathematical structure is identical to that of later associative memory networks.

In \citeyear{amari1972}, \citeauthor{amari1972} made this recurrent architecture adaptive , enabling it to learn to associate input patterns with output patterns by changing its connection weights, creating the first published learning recurrent neural network.
Ten years later, the basic equations of Amari's network were republished and its storage capacity analyzed under the name “Hopfield Network.”
Warren Sturgis McCulloch was born on 16 November 1898 in Orange, New Jersey, into a family of Scottish descent.

His mother, Mary Hughes Bradley, was devoutly Episcopalian and hoped he would enter the ministry; at the Carteret Academy he memorised poetry and set up a basement laboratory for what he later called “endless experiments, some with happy, others with catastrophic results.” In 1917 he entered Haverford College, a Quaker liberal-arts college near Philadelphia, where the philosopher Rufus M.
Jones encouraged his interest in mathematics and philosophy.
He moved to Yale for the Navy's officers' training programme — he never saw active service — and took a philosophy major with psychology; at Columbia he took an M.A.

in psychology with a thesis on “dynamic symmetry,” Jay Hambidge's claim that the golden-section rectangle is the most pleasing proportion, which McCulloch tested on fellow students with picture cards.
In 1924 he married Ruth “Rook” Metzger; they bought a run-down farm in Old Lyme, Connecticut, which became first a children's summer camp and then a working farm.
From 1932 he worked at Rockland State Hospital, where he met Eilhard von Domarus and began to treat psychiatric illness as a logical disturbance.
Six years in Dusser de Barenne's laboratory at Yale followed; in 1941 he moved to the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute, where he met Jerome Lettvin and Walter Pitts.
He chaired the Macy conferences, moved to MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics in 1952, and died in Old Lyme on 24 September 1969, leaving his body to Yale.
Ralph Gerard's obituary called him a “rebel genius” (\cite[Abraham, 2016]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
The question he said drove him — “What is a number, that a man may know it, and a man, that he may know a number?” — he later dated to a conversation with a teacher at Haverford in 1917.

Abraham treats that origin story with caution: McCulloch was an intellectual showman who constructed his autobiography over decades, and the anecdote is best read as a retrospective framing of the epistemological question, not as a verbatim memory (\cite{mcculloch1965embodiments, abraham2016rebelgenius}).
The paper's intellectual home was the mathematical-biophysics group at the University of Chicago, even though the byline names the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute.
The reason the paper exists at all was a Russian theoretical physicist named Nicolas Rashevsky (1899–1972).

Rashevsky arrived in Chicago in 1934 and set out to build a mathematical biology on the model of mathematical physics: begin with deliberately idealized systems — the biological equivalents of the physicist's “material point” and “ideal fluid” — and approach real organisms asymptotically.
In 1939 he founded the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, initially a supplement to *Psychometrika*, and around him gathered Alston S.
Landahl, and the young Walter Pitts.
Their nerve-net models were written in differential equations, with continuous excitation and inhibition.
McCulloch and Pitts published in that Bulletin, and their move was a discrete turn within it.
Where Rashevsky modeled the graded electrical state of the membrane, they took the all-or-none law literally and replaced the differential equations with propositional logic.
McCulloch later said that they were able to publish “thanks to Rashevsky's defense of logical and mathematical ideas in biology” (\cite[Abraham, 2002]{abraham2002physio}).

The contrast is the point: the 1943 paper was not Rashevsky's biophysics dressed in logic, but a logical turn inside the space Rashevsky had opened (\cite{rashevsky1936psychometrika, abraham2002physio}).
McCulloch's half of the collaboration was empirical.

At Yale he spent six years in the laboratory of the Dutch physiologist Johannes Gregorius Dusser de Barenne (1885–1940), who mapped functional connections in the cerebral cortex by applying small squares of paper soaked in strychnine — “chemical neuronography” — instead of the usual electrical stimulation.

McCulloch co-authored more than twenty papers with him, and the lab's program was exactly what McCulloch meant by “experimental epistemology”: a physiological theory of knowledge, not a philosophical one.

When Dusser died in 1940, McCulloch moved to the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute in Chicago, invited by Percival Bailey, and it was there — as professor of psychiatry — that he met Pitts (\cite{abraham2002physio, abraham2003mcculloch}).
McCulloch's question was epistemological before it was computational.

In the 1920s he set out to invent “a kind of least psychic event, or ‘psychon’” with four properties: it either happens or does not; it happens only if its bound cause has happened, so that it implies its temporal antecedent; it proposes this to subsequent psychons; and psychons compound into the equivalents of more complicated propositions.
Around 1929 he realized that the all-or-none impulse of a neuron fit the description.
The 1943 paper says it outright: “a psychon can be no less than the activity of a single neuron” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}).
The logical neuron is therefore not a metaphor for the mind; it is McCulloch's candidate for the atom of experience (\cite{mcculloch1965embodiments, abraham2002physio}).
The psychiatric route into the paper is easy to miss.
In 1932 McCulloch was training at Rockland State Hospital, where he met the German-born psychiatrist Eilhard von Domarus (1893–1958).
Von Domarus had written a Yale dissertation under F.

Northrop — *The Logical Structure of Mind* (\cite[Von Domarus, 1930]{domarus1930logicalstructure}) — with McCulloch's help, and in 1939 he presented “The specific laws of logic in schizophrenia” (\cite[Von Domarus, 1944]{domarus1944specificlaws}), arguing that delusional thought follows its own inferential rules.

Northrop, a philosopher of science at Yale, held that every empirical science matures from an inductive, descriptive stage into a deductive, axiomatic one; biology, he thought, was making that transition through J.
Woodger's *The Axiomatic Method in Biology* (\cite{woodger1937axiomatic}) and Rashevsky's mathematical biophysics.
McCulloch moved in that circle — he also attended Clark Hull's Wednesday-evening seminar at Yale in 1936 — and the result is a paper that treats mental illness as a logical disturbance.

Its final section lists tinnitus, paraesthesias, hallucinations, delusions, confusion and disorientation as what happens when the net is altered, and concludes that “diseased mentality can be understood without loss of scope or rigor, in the scientific terms of neurophysiology” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}; \cite{northrop1931sciencefirstprinciples, abraham2002physio}).
Walter Pitts grew up in a tough family in Prohibition-era Detroit.
His father, a boiler-maker, wanted him out of school and at work; Pitts taught himself Greek, Latin, logic and mathematics in the public library instead.
At twelve he read all three volumes of *Principia Mathematica*, found mistakes in it, and wrote to Bertrand Russell; Russell replied and invited him to Cambridge, but Pitts was too young to go.
At fifteen he ran away from home, headed for Chicago to hear Russell lecture, and never saw his family again.
He was homeless, self-taught and without a degree when he met McCulloch \cite{gefter2015pitts}.

Neil Smalheiser, who collected reminiscences of Pitts, calls him a “shadowy folk hero” of the brain-as-computer idea — a man who helped change several fields and was then largely forgotten \cite{smalheiser2000pitts}.
What they discovered in their first conversation was a shared hero: Gottfried Leibniz, whose “alphabet of human thought” promised to encode concepts as symbols and combine them by logical rules.
McCulloch was trying to build a Leibnizian calculus for the brain; Pitts knew the logic needed to make it work (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
Warren McCulloch came from a well-to-do East Coast family of lawyers, doctors, theologians and engineers.
He studied mathematics at Haverford, philosophy and psychology at Yale, and medicine at Columbia.

Tara Abraham's biography calls him an “intellectual showman” who adopted many identities — philosopher, poet, neurologist, neuropsychiatrist, cybernetician, mentor, engineer \cite{abraham2016rebelgenius}.

Gefter's portrait describes him as a “confident, gray-eyed, wild-bearded, chain-smoking philosopher-poet who lived on whiskey and ice cream and never went to bed before 4 a.m.” He wrote poetry, hosted bohemian evenings at his farm in Old Lyme — where he also designed buildings and a dam — and posted a sign on the door of his MIT lab reading “Experimental Epistemology.” When he met Pitts, he invited the homeless teenager to live with his family in Hinsdale.

The house was a bohemian salon of Chicago intellectuals, poetry, radical politics and Spanish Civil War songs; late at night, after the household had gone to bed, the two worked on a logical model of the brain \cite{gefter2015pitts}.
“Experimental Epistemology” was not a joke.
McCulloch wanted to know what it means to know, and he treated the brain as the place where that question could be answered experimentally.
Raised in a family of theologians and trained in philosophy before medicine, he never saw the mind as a merely technical problem.

His essays were collected in *Embodiments of Mind* (1965), and one of them asks the question that drove him: “What is a number, that a man may know it, and a man, that he may know a number?” \cite{mcculloch1965embodiments}.

Abraham's study of his years at the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute argues that the 1943 paper grew out of this project — out of a mathematical treatment of biological problems, not out of a plan to build a thinking machine — and that his identities as neuropsychiatrist and cybernetician were inseparable \cite{abraham2003mcculloch, abraham2016rebelgenius}.

His 1945 paper “A Heterarchy of Values Determined by the Topology of Nervous Nets” made the point that value is not a hierarchy: depending on the state of the network, A can be preferred to B, B to C, and C to A \cite{mcculloch1945heterarchy}.
Pitts supplied the mathematics McCulloch lacked: modular arithmetic for the loops, and the propositional calculus for the logic.

Their 1943 paper gave the field its first logical neuron and, in McCulloch's words, let him say “for the first time in the history of science, we know how we know” \cite{gefter2015pitts, mccullochpitts1943, abraham2002physio}.
McCulloch called Pitts his “bootlegged collaborator” and wrote of him, “Would I had him with me always.” Pitts called McCulloch's house home for the rest of his life.
Both men wrote poetry; a poem of Pitts's, “On Quantity of Information,” survives in McCulloch's papers.
The paper's influence ran wider than the perceptron.

Wiener was so impressed that he promised Pitts a PhD at MIT even though Pitts had never finished high school; in 1954 Fortune named Pitts one of the twenty most talented scientists under forty, alongside Claude Shannon and James Watson \cite{gefter2015pitts}.

Inside the group his authority was absolute: McCulloch wrote that none of them would publish a paper without Pitts's corrections and approval, and Lettvin called him “the genius of our group” (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
Pitts had struggled with depression for years.

He described it to McCulloch as a “melancholy apathy” that made “the positive value seem to disappear from the world,” and traced it partly to an “excessively logical education” that left him unable to believe in induction — “one cannot prove,” he wrote, “that the sun should rise tomorrow.” His dissertation was an attempt to make the logical brain statistical: since genes cannot specify the brain's trillions of synapses, he reasoned, the brain might start as a random net and let experience alter thresholds until order emerged (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).

Two blows deepened the depression: a break with Norbert Wiener, who had been a father figure, and the frog's-eye experiments, which showed that the retina already extracts contrast, curvature and movement before the brain gets involved — evidence that the brain was not the clean logical machine he had modeled.
The experiments became “What the Frog's Eye Tells the Frog's Brain” (1959), by Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch and Pitts (\cite{lettvin1959frog}).

The byline is misleading: the year of single-fibre recording was Lettvin's and Maturana's work, and McCulloch and Pitts joined the paper, in Lettvin's recollection, largely out of respect (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp.
163–164]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).

The break with Wiener has been traced, in secondhand accounts, to a story his wife told him about Pitts and Lettvin; Wiener never asked them, and never spoke to Pitts again (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
He began drinking heavily, refused to sign the paperwork for his doctorate on probabilistic three-dimensional neural networks, burned the manuscript and his notes, and withdrew from nearly everyone.
McCulloch died four months later, in September 1969 \cite{gefter2015pitts, smalheiser2000pitts}.

Pitts and McCulloch's 1947 follow-up proposed that the visual cortex extracts an invariant by averaging over a group of transformations — dilations, translations — so that the form “triangle” survives changes in size and position.
McCulloch presented the programme at the Hixon Symposium in September 1948 as “Why the Mind Is in the Head,” and the reaction was hostile.

Karl Lashley objected that the theory explained a behaviour “that never occurs in the intact organism”; Wolfgang Köhler called its histological assumptions ad hoc and accused McCulloch of using psychological terms “in a diluted sense”; John Eccles said McCulloch's imagination and verbal imagery ran away with the argument.
McCulloch's reply, recalled by Seymour Papert, was: “Don't bite my finger — look where I am pointing.”
The decisive blow came from inside McCulloch's own laboratory.

Donald MacKay built a square that could be expanded, shrunk at any speed, or fed back into the subject's own brain waves; by McCulloch's account it should have destroyed the ability to perceive form, and it did not.
Lashley's histological evidence pointed the same way.

McCulloch took falsification seriously: “To insist on an error is to insist that there is something to be tested.” The episode is a useful corrective to the usual founder story: the 1943 neuron was a permanent contribution, but McCulloch's own theory of universals was wrong, and he knew it (\cite{pitts1947universals, abraham2016rebelgenius}).
Von Neumann saw the catch early.

After “the great positive contribution of Turing-cum-Pitts-and-McCulloch is assimilated,” he wrote to Wiener, “the situation is rather worse than better than before”: the paper had shown, “in absolute and hopeless generality,” that any behaviour could be produced by some neural mechanism, and therefore that a general mechanism gave no clue about the details of the actual neural mechanism.

The universality that made the model powerful also made it unfalsifiable as neuroscience — one reason it made “barely a ripple among brain scientists” while it quietly became the blueprint for computing (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).

In 1937, a 21-year-old MIT graduate student named Claude Elwood Shannon submitted his master's thesis, \cite[*A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits*]{shannon1937switching}, which demonstrated that the two-valued Boolean algebra developed by \citeauthor{bool1854} in 1854 could serve as a theoretical foundation for the design of electrical switching circuits.
Shannon recognized that the binary states of electrical relay switches, open or closed, on or off, were isomorphic to the truth values of Boolean logic: true and false, 1 and 0.
Any arrangement of series and parallel switches could be described by a Boolean expression, and conversely, any Boolean expression could be physically realized as a circuit of relays.
His thesis laid the foundations for all digital computing and digital circuits.

The utilization of the binary properties of electrical switches to perform logic functions is the basic concept that underlies all electronic digital computer designs, from the earliest relay computers to the GPU clusters training today's large language models.

A \citeyear{poirier2025neat} historical study \cite{poirier2025neat} shows that the Symbolic AI program was never unified to begin with.
From the 1960s through the 1990s, knowledge-representation researchers sorted themselves into two camps that Poirier traces back to a methodological, then an aesthetic, opposition.
The **logicists** (“neats”) gathered around **McCarthy at Stanford** and traced their intellectual lineage to \citeauthor{frege1879}; Frege himself died in 1925 and was never at Stanford.
They pursued McCarthy's program of expressing everyday knowledge in formal, declarative logic and drawing conclusions by predicate calculus.

The **proceduralists** (“scruffies”) gathered around Minsky at MIT and were willing to tolerate paradox, hand-coded heuristics, and incomplete representations in exchange for systems that actually worked on messy problems.
Patrick Hayes, interviewed by Poirier, summarizes the split bluntly: the classical line-up was Minsky versus McCarthy, and he adds that this is very much an oversimplification.
Minsky's 1974 paper “A Framework for Representing Knowledge,” which introduced **frames** as stereotyped data structures, was the scruffy camp's counter-move to pure logic.

By the 1990s most knowledge architects concluded both approaches were necessary, but by then the field had spent two decades unable to deliver commonsense reasoning, and the resulting loss of confidence, not the Perceptrons book alone, is what tipped AI into its first winter.

The neat/scruffy split is also why the Minsky who co-authored the devastating critique of perceptrons was *not*, in this earlier frame, an enemy of neural networks; he was the champion of the *procedural* wing of symbolic AI against McCarthy's *logicist* wing.

He drowned on July 11, 1971, his forty-third birthday, while sailing his sloop *Shearwater* on Chesapeake Bay (\cite[Lefkowitz, 2019]{lefkowitz2019perceptron}; \cite[Emlen et al., 1971]{rosenblattmemorial1971}).

Based on the \citealternativetitle{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour}, idea of the canadian psychology professor \citeauthor{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour} published that neurons in the brain get a stronger connection to each other when they often fire together, which is often expressed as “neurons that fire together, wire together”, and the idea of neurons proposed by \citeauthorlastnameand{mccullochpitts1943}, in \citeyear{rosenblatt1958perceptron}, **\citeauthor{rosenblatt1958perceptron}** introduced the **Perceptron**, the biological-inspired ancestor of the modern neuron.
Shifting away from rigid symbolic logic, he proposed a system that could “learn” by automatically adjusting its weights in response to errors.
This marked a pivotal transition from hard-coded programming to the foundational principles of machine learning.
The HNF blog's history of the McCulloch–Pitts paper follows their 1943 “logical calculus” from that first mathematical neuron to the networks that followed \cite{hnfmccullochpitts2023}.

Dunning reconstructs the Mark I from the perspective of Thomas Osborn, a Cornell undergraduate hired as a “worker bee” at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo to solder its six-foot racks in the fall of 1959.
The architecture mapped a 20×20 grid of photocell “S-units” onto **512** association units, whose connections were generated as genuinely random numbers on CAL's IBM 704 and then wired by hand.

Each A-unit's output passed through a motor-driven potentiometer whose wiper voltage could swing continuously between −11 and +11 V, so “between zero and one there was any number in-between”: the “memory” of the machine was literally the angle of 512 little motors, updated automatically by the feedback loop.

The single most striking finding from the testing phase was empirical: introducing a deliberate rate of **forgetting** (resistors allowed to decay slightly between iterations) dramatically sped up learning by preventing the network from overfitting idiosyncrasies of the first few examples, an early, hardware-level instance of what would later be formalized as weight decay.

The Mark I never served its intended Pentagon mission of spotting Soviet missile sites from aerial photographs, but Osborn could train it to around 90–95% accuracy on letter recognition, and the team agreed it had done “what it said it was going to do.” After Osborn left Buffalo, “no one said one word to me about it”; he went on to become a quantum physicist at the University of Manitoba, a quiet reminder that landmark devices are also the product of anonymous assembly work.

A \citeyear{lindquist2026weirdai} \cite{lindquist2026weirdai} in the same “Think Piece” department argues that midcentury neural-AI architects (Rosenblatt, then Rumelhart, Hinton, McClelland and the PDP group in the 1980s) deliberately engineered **nonrationality** into their machines rather than stumbling onto it.
Lindquist reads the perceptron, and later PDP, as part of a Romantic countercurrent inside computing, a refusal to reduce thought to logical manipulation.

In the original \citeyear{darthmouthartificialintelligence} proposal, IBM engineer **Nathaniel Rochester** himself argued that introducing randomness into neural networks could foster originality, comparing the effect to dreaming or intoxication.
When Minsky and Papert wrote in \citetitle{minskyperceptrons} that perceptron work was “romantic,” they meant it as a *critique*; the PDP community later wore the label as a badge of pride.

What we now dismiss as LLM “hallucinations,” Lindquist points out, is essentially the same property midcentury researchers deliberately prized: outputs landing in the thin tails of the probability distribution, the unreliability from which surprising new associations were supposed to emerge.

Modern accounts that frame today's neural nets as a product of “big data and GPUs” alone miss that the original appeal of the architecture was never just pattern-matching; it was a wager that a machine which occasionally did the unexpected could be more useful than one which never did.

The Pāṇinian line of structural linguistics reaches its otherworldly culmination in a single short book, \citetitle{tesniere1959deps} (\citeyear{tesniere1959deps}), written by the French linguist \citeauthor{tesniere1959deps} (\citeyear{tesniere1959deps}) and published posthumously five years after his death.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: Tesnière's central claim is that the basic unit of syntactic description is not the **phrase** (as in Pāṇini's phrase-structure rules and in Chomsky's later constituent-structure trees) but the **dependency relation**: a directed link from a *governor* word to a *dependent* word.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: A sentence is, on this view, a **stemma** — a tree of word-to-word dependencies, with the main verb at the root and each word hanging directly off the word whose meaning it modifies, with no intermediate phrasal nodes.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: A simple sentence like "the cat sat on the mat" is one verb (*sat*) with three dependents (*the cat*, its subject; *on the mat*, its prepositional complement), each of which carries its own dependents (*the* on *cat*, *the* on *mat*).
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: What is striking about Tesnière's framework is how much modern NLP silently inherits from it.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: Constituent-structure trees dominated the syntactic theory of the 1960s–80s and underlie most formal grammars, but the dependency view turned out to be a better match for the kinds of *local* relations that matter in practice — who is the subject of which verb, which noun does a pronoun refer to, which preposition links which argument — and modern dependency parsers now dominate the field.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The Stanford, Universal Dependencies, spaCy, and Stanza parsers all produce exactly Tesnière's dependency trees, with typed governor→dependent relations like `nsubj`, `dobj`, `amod`, `prep`; Universal Dependencies' 200+ typologically diverse languages are precisely the kind of cross-linguistic coverage Tesnière would have wanted.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The two are also formally equivalent in a precise sense: a constituent-structure tree can be derived from a dependency tree (by collapsing chains of head-dependent relations into phrasal nodes), and a *projective* dependency tree can be derived from a constituent-structure tree (by reading off the head of each constituent).
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The difference is not in *what can be expressed*; it is in *what is taken as primitive*, and on that question, the modern NLP field has voted for Tesnière.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The deeper lesson is methodological.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: Tesnière's book appeared in 1959, only two years after Chomsky's *Syntactic Structures* (1957) and before Chomsky's constituent-structure frame had become dominant in generative linguistics — but the dependency idea was not new with him; it had been sketched by the Sanskrit grammarians, by the Roman *modistae*, and by Lucien Tesnière's own predecessors.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The reason the framework is taking *forty years* to mature in NLP is partly that the computational tools needed to parse at scale (transition-based parsers, neural parsers, large dependency-banks) only became available in the 2000s, and partly that the *training data* — sentences annotated with dependency relations — only became widely available in 2014 with the Universal Dependencies project.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar — French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The progress curve of dependency parsing looks, on the chart, much like the progress curve of every other old AI idea: the framework existed for decades; the right *representation* and *learning algorithm* took decades more; the moment it became usable, every system quietly switched to it.

The deepest *theoretical* foundation of modern machine learning was laid by two mathematicians working in the Soviet Union, largely unnoticed in the West.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: Their programme began in the early 1960s, when \citeauthor{vapnik1964vc} was at the Institute for Control Sciences in Moscow; in 1971 they published, in *Teoriya Veroyatnostei i ee Primeneniya* (translated as *Theory of Probability and Its Applications*), the paper that introduced the **VC dimension** and the **VC inequality**: a precise, distribution-free upper bound on the *generalisation error* of a classifier trained on $n$ samples, in terms of a single property of the classifier's *hypothesis class* — the largest set the class can *shatter* (correctly label in every possible way).
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: A classifier that can shatter $d$ points needs roughly $n \gtrsim d/\varepsilon$ labelled examples to reach error $\varepsilon$ on new data; a classifier that cannot shatter any set of size $d$ is *restricted* and generalises from correspondingly fewer.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: The bound holds for *every* distribution, makes *no* parametric assumptions, and is *tight* — there are constructions showing that no purely combinatorial bound can do better.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: The result is the first general theorem of statistical learning that gives an engineer a *numerical* answer to the question "how much data do I need?" without requiring the engineer to know the underlying distribution.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: The Anglo-American ML community did not learn of the result for nearly twenty-five years.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: The Russian-language paper sat in a Soviet journal behind a language barrier and a Cold-War travel barrier; the related 1974 monograph (*The Theory of Pattern Recognition*, in Russian) reached only those who read Russian.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: By the time the result crossed the Iron Curtain, in the late 1970s and 1980s (through personal contacts, translations by Vapnik's collaborators, and the slow internationalisation of the field), the connectionist community was already fully invested in *empirical* "generalisation is just running on a held-out set" approaches, and the *theoretical* community was absorbed with PAC-learning, Bayesian model comparison, and statistical-decision theory.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: It took Vapnik's move to Bell Labs in 1990, his joint work with Cortes on the **support vector machine** (1995), and the publication of *The Nature of Statistical Learning Theory* (1995, English) to make VC theory *the* theoretical backbone of kernel methods, regularisation theory, and modern generalisation bounds.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: From the late 1990s onward, VC theory became standard textbook material — *Understanding Machine Learning* by Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Bishop's *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning*, Mohri's *Foundations of Machine Learning* — but the original contribution, published in 1971, sat for a generation unread in the West.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: The Cold-War provenance matters for this chapter's deeper story.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: The 1960s and 1970s Soviet AI tradition was not a *single* programme; it was *three* parallel programmes, one in each of the three subfields this chapter traces.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: In **deep learning**, \citeauthor{vapnik1964vc}'s colleagues \citeauthor{ivakhnenko1965} and his collaborators in Kyiv were building GMDH networks.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: In **pattern recognition**, \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern} at the Moscow IITP was solving Bongard problems.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: In **statistical learning theory**, \citeauthor{vapnik1964vc} in Moscow was formalising the generalisation bound.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: All three programmes were funded, conducted, and published in Russian; all three were *unknown* to the Anglophone AI community for one or two decades; all three were *rediscovered* and integrated into mainstream ML between 1985 and 2010.
statements.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory — The Soviet Cold-War Secret

statements.quote: The Anglosphere's contribution — Rosenblatt's perceptron, Widrow's ADALINE, Rumelhart's backpropagation, LeCun's ConvNets, Hinton's deep belief nets, Sutskever's sequence-to-sequence — is more *visible* in the standard history because the network effects of English-language publication were enormous, but it is not *larger* in mathematical content.

statements.quote: The Soviet trio — Ivakhnenko, Bongard, Vapnik — produced the three pieces of the modern ML stack the Anglophone tradition did *not* independently produce, and the 1990s integration of all three lines is the moment "machine learning" became a single field.

statements.quote: Traditional methods for finding optimal flight paths relied on complex differential equations (**Euler-Lagrange**) that were nearly impossible to solve for real-world missions.
They often failed to satisfy “two-point boundary conditions”, meaning you couldn't easily force the math to start at Point A and end exactly at Point B.
\citeauthor{kelley} proposed a **“Direct Method”** (Steepest Descent):
**Start with a guess:** Pick any flight path that hits the start and end points.
**Find the Gradient:** Calculate the direction of steepest improvement (e.g., less time/fuel).
**Stepwise Update:** Shift the path slightly in that direction.
**Iterate:** Repeat until the path converges to the mathematical optimum.
This paper is a foundational application of **Gradient Descent**, the engine of modern AI:
* **Loss Minimization:** In the paper, the “Error” is extra flight time; in NNs, “Loss” is the prediction error.
* **Weight Updates:** Just as Kelley adjusted flight parameters (thrust/angle) in small steps, NNs adjust their weights using the same “steepest descent” logic.
* **Learning Rate:** The paper's “step size” ($\Delta\sigma$) is exactly what we now call the **Learning Rate** in deep learning.
This paper is now recognized as a direct **precursor of backpropagation**.

Kelley's method backpropagated derivative information through standard Jacobian matrix calculations from one “stage” to the previous one, anticipating the core logic of the algorithm that would later be generalized by \citeauthor{linnainmaa1970} in \citeyear{linnainmaa1970} and eventually become the foundation of all modern deep learning.
See also the related early 1960s work of Stuart Dreyfus and Arthur E.
Bryson in control theory.
While AI research suffered through funding winters, the physical substrate of computing was undergoing an explosion.
\citealternativetitle{mooreslaw} describes the observation made by Gordon Moore that the number of transistors in a dense integrated circuit doubles about every two years.
This relentless exponential growth meant that while algorithms remained largely unchanged for decades, the machinery running them became millions of times more powerful.

This “free” improvement in performance is the engine behind \citetitle{sutton2019bitter}: methods that scale with computation (like neural networks) were destined to eventually overtake methods that relied on human cleverness, simply because the hardware kept getting faster.
While the popularization of backpropagation is often credited to the 1980s, its mathematical genesis lies in the 1970 master's thesis of \citeauthor{linnainmaa1970}.
He developed the “automatic differentiation” method, specifically the *reverse mode*, originally to efficiently manage rounding errors in complex computer calculations.
Without explicitly intending it for neural networks, Linnainmaa created the highly efficient algorithm required to calculate gradients in nested functions.
This work serves as the invisible mathematical backbone of modern Deep Learning, allowing error signals to be propagated backward through billions of parameters with minimal computational overhead.
Long before neural networks, a different kind of computing was pushing the hardware forward: the computers that flew.

statements.quote: A spacecraft computer could not crash, could not be powered off, and could not be handed to a technician who walked over and pressed *reset* — so NASA's spaceflight programs forced the industry into **real-time, fault-tolerant** design decades before it became mainstream.
statements.section: NASA Spaceflight Computers: Real-Time Reliability in Orbit (1965–1989)

statements.quote: Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published their book \citetitle{minskyperceptrons}, which provided a mathematical proof of the architecture's limitations.
They demonstrated that a single-layer perceptron could not solve the **XOR (Exclusive OR)** problem because it was not “linearly separable.”
To understand why the XOR problem was so significant, we first need to look at how a computer processes logic.
We can represent logical gates as functions that take an input matrix (representing all possible combinations of two inputs) and map them to an output vector.
* **False** is represented as $0$ (red) and
* **True** is represented $1$ (green)
The **OR** gate is “True” if at least one input is “True.”
The **XOR** gate is “True” *only* if the inputs are different.

Minsky and Papert demonstrated that while a single-layer perceptron can draw a line to separate the results of an OR gate, it is mathematically impossible to do so for XOR because the “True” and “False” results are not **linearly separable**.
Long before Lighthill's report, a Heideggerian philosopher at Berkeley had been telling AI researchers that their entire program was misconceived.

\citeauthor{dreyfus1972what}'s 1972 \citetitle{dreyfus1972what} attacked symbolic AI from the side of phenomenology: expert skill, Dreyfus argued, is not a collection of rules the expert could in principle articulate, but a holistic, situated, often pre-reflective responsiveness to context.

The 1960s AI optimism that “thinking” could be formalized as symbol manipulation therefore missed what thinking actually is, a position he sharpened in seminars at Berkeley that AI faculty and graduate students were essentially required to attend, since Dreyfus taught in the Philosophy Department next door.

The AI community's classical counter (that AI would succeed once enough rules were collected) looks, in retrospect, like the precise pattern Sutton would later diagnose as the loser in the bitter lesson.
Dreyfus's 1992 *What Computers Still Can't Do*, written after the second AI winter, was widely read as a vindication.
**Leon Harmon** (1922–1983) was a Bell Labs vision researcher who spent the 1970s trying to teach machines to see faces.
He had wired the IAS machine for Julian Bigelow in 1950, met von Neumann and Einstein there, and joined Bell Labs in 1956, where he worked on human perception, computer vision and graphics.
With Ken Knowlton he made *Studies in Perception I* (1966), a photomosaic of the dancer Deborah Hay assembled from typographic symbols; it was printed in the *New York Times* in 1967.

His best-known image is the pixelated Lincoln from the five-dollar bill, made for his 1973 *Scientific American* article "The Recognition of Faces" — a demonstration that a face survives even when it is reduced to a coarse grid.
Dalí later used it in *Lincoln in Dalivision* (\cite{harmon1973faces}; \cite{harmonwiki}).

Harmon's "artificial eye" was less a single device than a research programme: machine recognition of faces, profiles and print, and the use of degraded images to find out what human vision needs (\cite{harmonwiki}).
He was also one of the field's sharpest internal critics.

In a 1981 *Christian Science Monitor* essay, "Artificial intelligence: accent is on artificial," he wrote that "most artificial-intelligence (AI) systems do trivial things impressively": chess, face recognition, constrained dialogue and medical diagnosis worked because their domains had been sharply restricted, while generalization, semantics, autonomy and creativity remained out of reach.

The essay is a useful corrective to the usual winter narrative: the skepticism did not come only from philosophers and funding agencies, but from a vision researcher who had built some of the demos himself (\cite[Harmon, 1981]{harmon1981ai}).

Before LeCun perfected the CNN, the architectural blueprints were drawn by **Kunihiko Fukushima** (who, in turn, based his work in the work of \citeauthorlastnameand{hubelwiesel}, who researched the cat's visual cortex), in \citeyear{neocognitron}, he developed the **\citealternativetitle{neocognitron}**, a hierarchical network inspired by the visual cortex.

It introduced the two key layers of modern vision AI: “S-cells” (simple) for feature extraction and “C-cells” (complex) for pooling, which allowed the machine to recognize objects even if they were shifted in position.

The full argument sits in Rosenblatt's 1961 Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory report, \citetitle{rosenblattbackprop} (16 March 1961), a book-length synthesis of the perceptron program that runs from the biological motivation through three-layer series-coupled systems to multi-layer, cross-coupled and speculative models.

Its §13.3 is the "back-propagating error correction procedure": the error of the response units is assigned back to the association units by a probabilistic rule, and the connections are then corrected exactly as in the elementary perceptron.

It is not backpropagation as modern deep learning knows it — there is no gradient, no chain rule, and the credit assignment is stochastic — but the name and the central intuition that an output error can be pushed back into earlier layers are already there.

Chapter 13 of the 1962 book added layer-wise learning rates, bypass connections, and multimodal variants; the heuristics did not work reliably because the step nonlinearity inherited from the threshold neuron had no usable gradient (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}).
The Defense Technical Information Center's scan is available in full at the Internet Archive.
However, these deep structures were difficult to train until the popularization of **Backpropagation** by \citeauthor{rumelhart1986} in \citeyear{rumelhart1986}.
This mathematical technique allowed the “error” of a network to be sent backward through the layers, adjusting the weights with precision.
The combination of Fukushima's architecture and Rumelhart's training algorithm set the stage for the deep learning revolution.
While early neural networks were limited, **Yann LeCun et al** revolutionized computer vision by developing the first practical **Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)**.
In \citeyear{lecun1989backpropagation}, LeCun combined convolutions with backpropagation to recognize handwritten ZIP codes for the U.S.
Postal Service, an early influential demonstration of a backprop-trained convolutional network.
In \citeyear{lecun1998gradientbased}, he introduced **LeNet-5**, the refined architecture for recognizing handwritten digits (and, later, bank checks).
Unlike standard networks, CNNs use small, learnable filters to automatically extract spatial features like edges and shapes.
This proved that biological inspiration, mimicking the visual cortex, could solve complex pattern recognition tasks that traditional logic-based AI could not.
The popular attribution of the CNN to LeCun overlooks substantial earlier work, which \citeauthor{schmidhuber2025cnn} documents in detail.

**Kunihiko Fukushima** introduced a rectified linear activation in \citeyear{fukushima1969relu} — a direct precursor of the ReLU that powers essentially every modern Transformer — and the basic **Neocognitron** architecture with alternating convolutional and downsampling layers in \citeyear{neocognitron}, inspired by Hubel and Wiesel's cat visual-cortex work.

**Alex Waibel**, a German researcher in Japan, trained supervised one-dimensional convolutional NNs with weight-sharing (TDNNs) on Linnainmaa's 1970 backpropagation in \citeyear{waibel1987tdnn} for speech recognition, and introduced the term *convolution* into NNs.

**Wei Zhang** at Osaka then built the first *modern* two-dimensional CNN trained by backpropagation in \citeyear{zhang1988cnn}, applied to character recognition — one year *before* LeCun's 1989 Bell Labs paper, and LeCun's widely read 1998 survey does not cite it.
LeCun's contribution was nevertheless substantial.
His 1989 Bell Labs work combined backpropagation with convolutions on handwritten ZIP codes for the U.S.
Postal Service — a research prototype that showed the approach could work end-to-end.
His 1998 **LeNet-5** refined the architecture for bank-check recognition and was the first robust, end-to-end backprop-trained system deployed on a real commercial OCR problem at scale.
The lineage runs from Fukushima's biological inspiration, through Zhang's and Waibel's first end-to-end CNNs, to LeCun's production-grade system; each step added something the earlier work had not.

Jürgen Schmidhuber's \citetitle{schmidhuber2022deep} documents a striking concentration of foundational ideas at his lab at TU Munich in the twelve months from early 1990 to mid 1991, a window worth knowing about in its own right.

In it the group published the principles for what we now call **generative adversarial networks** (a controller network in a zero-sum game with a predictor, February 1990); the first **subgoal-generating** networks for hierarchical reinforcement learning; and in 1991 a *fast-weight programmer* in which one neural network learns to slowly modify the weights of another — an abstraction Schmidhuber's group has connected to the learned key-query-value projections of the modern **Transformer**.

The same window saw unsupervised **pre-training** of deep neural networks; **knowledge distillation**, in which a small network is trained to mimic a larger one (the technique that underpins DeepSeek's compression of much larger frontier models); the formal identification of the **vanishing/exploding gradient** problem in Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis; and the **Long Short-Term Memory** architecture, gated recurrent residual connections that have since become one of the most cited AI papers ever published.

Several foundational ideas of modern deep learning — gated residual connections, fast-weight programmers, the GAN principle — can be traced to papers from this single window at a Bavarian technical university.

Schmidhuber has argued that the standard Anglophone narrative under-credits this European and Japanese work; other researchers in the field read the priorities more cautiously, and several of the cited innovations were independently rediscovered in different communities at different times.

Whatever position one takes on the priority disputes, the technical lineage itself is documented in the original papers and useful to know, because every modern AI system stands on at least some of these ideas.
The Fundamental Deep Learning Problem was identified and analyzed in \citeyear{hochreiter1991vanishing} by \citeauthor{hochreiter1991vanishing} in his diploma thesis supervised by Jürgen Schmidhuber.
He showed that in typical deep or recurrent networks, back-propagated error signals either shrink rapidly (vanish) or grow out of bounds (explode), making learning impossible for long sequences.

Crucially, Hochreiter derived from first principles the concept of a **recurrent residual connection**: a neural unit with the identity activation function connected to itself with weight 1.0, ensuring constant error flow across arbitrarily many time steps.
Building on this analysis, Schmidhuber coined the term **\citetitle{lstm}** in a 1995 tech report.
The main peer-reviewed publication of \citeyear{lstm} by \citeauthorlastnameand{lstm} is often described as the most cited AI paper of the 20th century.
A critical milestone was the **“vanilla LSTM” architecture with forget gates** (\citeyear{lstm_vanilla}), the variant that everybody uses today (e.g., in Google's TensorFlow).
It features gated recurrent residual connections whose gates are initially open (1.0), allowing the network to start with plain residual connections.
In \citeyear{ctc2006}, the training method **Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC)** was introduced for simultaneous alignment and recognition of sequences.
CTC-trained LSTM was successfully applied to speech in 2007 and became the first superior end-to-end neural speech recognizer.
In 2015, this CTC-LSTM combination **dramatically improved Google's speech recognition** on Android smartphones.
Google Translate (2016), whose technical paper mentions LSTM over 50 times, was based on two connected LSTMs.
By 2017, LSTM also powered Facebook's machine translation (over 30 billion translations per week), Apple's Quicktype on roughly 1 billion iPhones, and the voice of Amazon's Alexa.
LSTMs were the “workhorse” of AI for two decades (approx. 1997–2017).
Without the LSTM, the second AI Winter (early 1990s, triggered by the expert-systems bust) likely would have dragged neural NLP along with it for much longer.
It proved that connectionist models could handle the sequential, complex nature of human speech by implementing a form of persistent memory.
The most widely used neural language models of that era were based on LSTM as well, the transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) in the modern sense arrived with the GPT series (2018–2020).
A hands-on, visual tour of that two-decade workhorse — the loops, the gates, the vanishing gradients — lives in the [Networks with Memory chapter](recurrent_networks.php).
While Perceptrons attempted to mimic the brain's structure, a different approach focused on logic and brute-force search.
This “Symbolic AI” reached its zenith in May 1997, when **Deep Blue** won the six-game rematch against Kasparov; it had lost the 1996 match (\cite{deepblue}).
In a historic six-game rematch, IBM's Deep Blue defeated the reigning world chess champion, **Garry Kasparov**.
Unlike the learning-based Perceptron, Deep Blue relied on massive parallel processing capable of evaluating 200 million positions per second.
It proved that for well-defined logical problems, a machine could exceed human capability not through intuition, but through sheer computational calculation.
The match was broadcast live, and the win struck hard enough that IBM's share price briefly touched an all-time high \cite{toosi2021history}.
However, Deep Blue's victory represented the pinnacle of specific, hand-crafted logic rather than general intelligence.
While effective for the rigid rules of chess, relying on human-designed strategies proved to be a bottleneck for more complex, unstructured problems.
This realization leads directly to a fundamental, and somewhat painful, observation about the trajectory of AI progress.

The \citealternativetitle{shrdlu_image} (CC BY-SA 4.0, \citeauthor{shrdlu_image}) shows Terry Winograd's SHRDLU (1972), which answered typed questions about a virtual world of blocks — the canonical demonstration that natural-language reasoning over a small world was possible \cite{winograd1972understanding}.

A Deep Blue-class IBM chess machine at the Computer History Museum, from \citealternativetitle{deep_blue_image} ([CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/), \citeauthor{deep_blue_image}).
The Commons description notes that the computer shown is similar to, not identical with, the machine that beat Kasparov in 1997.
In 2003, **“\citetitle{neuralprobabilistic}”** by **Yoshua Bengio** and co-authors revived backpropagation for language modeling.
Their model replaced sparse n-gram tables with dense **word embeddings** \cite[first formalized in]{rumelhart1986pdp}, mapping semantic relationships into a continuous vector space.

Frameworks like **\cite[Torch]{collobert2002}**, **\cite[TensorFlow]{tensorflow2016}** and **\cite[PyTorch]{pytorch}** abstracted away manual differentiation and GPU memory management, allowing researchers to focus on architecture rather than implementation.

statements.quote: The fundamental difference lies in architecture.
A **CPU** (Central Processing Unit) is designed for **latency**: it has a few powerful cores optimized to do complex, sequential logic (MIMD: Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data).
It is like a professor who can solve difficult calculus problems one by one.

A **GPU** (Graphics Processing Unit), conversely, is designed for **throughput**: it has thousands of smaller, simpler cores designed to perform the same instruction on massive amounts of data simultaneously (SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data).
It is like a thousand elementary school students who can all perform simple addition at the exact same time.

Since training a neural network involves multiplying billions of floating-point numbers (weights) by billions of other numbers (inputs), the GPU's architecture allowed for speedups of **70x to 100x** over CPUs.
While early attempts to use GPUs for neural networks date back to **Oh & Jung** in \citeyear{oh2004gpu}, the breakthrough required a bridge between hardware and code.
This arrived with NVIDIA's release of **CUDA** in 2006, which allowed researchers to program GPUs without translating everything into “graphics” language.
* **The Scientific Proof:** In \citeyear{raina2009large}, a team at Stanford led by **Rajat Raina** and **Andrew Ng** published \citetitle{raina2009large}.
They demonstrated that off-the-shelf consumer GPUs (like the NVIDIA GeForce GTX 280) could train Deep Belief Networks orders of magnitude faster than multicore CPUs.
This paper quantified the “Bitter Lesson”: cheap hardware could replace complex algorithmic optimizations.
* **The Practical Proof:** In \citeyear{ciresan2011flexible}, **Dan Cireşan** and **Jürgen Schmidhuber** at IDSIA used this power to push the boundaries of what was possible.

Their system, “DanNet,” was the first pure GPU-based CNN to win international pattern recognition contests, beating human performance on tasks like traffic sign recognition years before the more famous AlexNet.
This hardware lottery, the fact that AI researchers could piggyback on the massive R&D budget of the gaming industry, is likely the single most important factor in the 21st-century AI boom.
The “Hardware Lottery” describes how the success of an idea depends less on its brilliance and more on whether it fits existing technology.
This is perfectly illustrated by **\citeauthor{weatherfactory}'s** **“\citealternativetitle{weatherfactory}”** (\citeyear{weatherfactory}).
Richardson envisioned a massive theater filled with 64,000 humans performing manual calculations (then called “computers”) in parallel to predict global weather.
While mathematically sound, it was a practical failure because human “hardware” was too slow and expensive to outpace the actual weather.
Just as Richardson's vision remained a “researcher's graveyard” until electronic computers arrived, **Deep Learning** remained relatively dormant in the 1980s.
The breakthrough wasn't mainly a new mathematical discovery, but the realization that **GPUs**, built for the gaming industry, were essentially Richardson's “Weather Factory” on a chip.
By using **SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data)** architecture, a single GPU could perform the work of thousands of sequential processors simultaneously.

This shifted AI from the slow, logical processing of a CPU to the massive throughput required for modern **LLMs**, finally providing the “hardware-friendly” environment Richardson's numerical methods always required.
**CUDA** (**Compute Unified Device Architecture**), introduced by NVIDIA in \citeyear{cuda}, revolutionized AI by enabling GPUs to perform general-purpose computations using standard C code.
This innovation unlocked GPUs' potential for parallel processing, crucial for tasks like matrix multiplications in neural networks.
For instance, AlexNet (2012) leveraged CUDA-enabled GPUs to train in days instead of years, marking a turning point in deep learning.
CUDA exemplifies the “Bitter Lesson” that scalable, compute-heavy methods outperform handcrafted algorithms over time.

The network, **AlexNet** (named after its leading author), was decisive not only for its depth but for a stack of then-unfashionable tricks: rectified-linear-unit (ReLU) activations and **dropout**, which together let it train far more layers end-to-end on raw pixels, with no hand-crafted features at all \cite{toosi2021history}.

The result was the birth of the third AI boom \cite{toosi2021history}, and it validated the \citealternativetitle{sutton2019bitter}: scale and computation ultimately triumph over hand-coded human intuition.
The connectionist revival was formally recognized in 2018, when the Turing Award went to Bengio, Hinton and LeCun for their pioneering work on deep learning \cite{toosi2021history}.

Before the modern Transformer, neural networks suffered from a “representational bottleneck.” Systems like the LSTM attempted to compress the entire meaning of a long sentence into a single, fixed-length vector, a task as impossible as summarizing a complex novel into a single word without losing the nuance.

statements.quote: Then came another breakthrough, the \citealternativetitle{vaswani2017attention}.
By utilizing a mechanism called **Self-Attention**, models could process entire sequences of data in parallel rather than word-by-word.
This mitigated the vanishing-gradient and long-range-dependency problems that had limited recurrent networks, and let models handle long context in text.
The further text will lead you through every step you need to understand this Self-Attention-Mechanism on a basic level.
The original goal of the Attention paper was not to build a chatbot, but to improve translation systems by a lot.
In this context, “attention” is a mathematical mechanism for weighting information, not a form of awareness or intent.
There is a second, quiet invention inside the same paper that is just as load-bearing, and it is easily overlooked.

Pure self-attention is **insensitive to word order**: it weighs every pair of tokens against every other, so a layer that has seen "the dog bites the man" and "the man bites the dog" sees, at its input, the same two clouds of tokens arranged differently — and would happily map both to the same output.
Language would collapse into a bag of words.

The authors solved this by adding **positional encodings** to every token: a deterministic pattern of sine and cosine waves overlaid on the embeddings so that each position in the sequence carries its own signature \cite{vaswani2017attention}.

Its descendants — learned position vectors, and later **rotary** embeddings (RoPE), which rotate pairs of embedding coordinates by an angle proportional to the position — remain inside every modern LLM.
Attention supplies the *what-goes-with-what*; positional encoding supplies the *where-it-was*, and both are needed, because neither order nor association alone is language.
The Attention Mechanism will be explained in detail later on.
The idea of modeling language statistically predates computers themselves.

At the end of the 1940s and the start of the 1950s, \citeauthor{shannon1948communication} applied information theory to English text, treating language as a stochastic process and asking how predictable the next symbol is.

His 1948 paper laid the mathematical foundation, and his 1951 paper on the entropy of printed English made the prediction view explicit: **n-gram models**, which predict the next word from the previous *n* words, could capture statistical regularities in language (\cite{shannon1948communication}; \cite{shannon1951communication}).
Through the 1980s and 1990s, n-gram-based statistical language models dominated speech recognition and machine translation, championed by researchers like Frederick Jelinek at IBM.

Meanwhile, **ELIZA** (1966), created by \citeauthorlastnameand{weizenbaum1976computer}, demonstrated early natural language interaction through simple pattern matching, but had no statistical understanding of language whatsoever.
Long before Shannon counted letters, so did the code-breakers.
The great Arab polymath \citeauthor{alkindi_cryptanalysis} (c.

801–873), in his *Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages*, invented **frequency analysis** \cite{historyofmath_wikipedia} \cite{alkindi_cryptanalysis}: count how often each symbol occurs in an intercepted message, compare the tallies against the known letter-frequencies of the language, and the ciphertext begins to crack itself.

That is a *statistical model of language* — the very insight Shannon's n-grams would formalize a thousand years later, and, ultimately, the one on which "predict the next word" rests: language carries measurable statistical structure, and that structure alone suffices to do useful work.
Frequency analysis is, in a real sense, the ninth-century great-grandparent of the language model — the point where the *counter* (al-Kindi) first out-performed the *rule-book* (Pāṇini).
The “stochastic parrot” framing reopens the oldest wound in the philosophy of AI.

In 1980, \citeauthor{searle1980minds} had proposed the **Chinese Room** thought experiment: imagine a person locked in a room who follows an English rule-book to shuffle incoming Chinese characters into outgoing Chinese characters.
From outside, the room behaves indistinguishably from a fluent Chinese speaker.
Yet the person inside understands nothing.
By Searle's argument, no amount of clever symbol-shuffling is sufficient for *understanding*; minds require specific biological machinery, what he calls *biological naturalism*.

The standard rebuttals in the AI literature (the *systems reply*: the room-plus-rules understands; the *robot reply*: grounding in a body fixes the problem; the *connectionist reply*: a neural net would not have the problem) all attempt to push the “understanding” somewhere outside the formal manipulation.

\citeauthor{russell2021aima} point out that Searle's argument is *not* an argument against AI as a field: even if no digital computer literally understands Chinese, AI systems can still be made to behave as if they do, and that behaviour is what the field optimises for.
The question the Chinese Room leaves unresolved is whether there is a meaningful difference between these two outcomes, and whether the distinction, if it exists, can be settled empirically at all.
LLMs in 2026 have not answered it; they have only made the question louder.
The emergence of ChatGPT represents the “Great Convergence” of a multi-millennial effort to decouple human thought from biology and translate it into formal abstraction.
